prompt: A cart already holds $7$ pounds of equipment and can carry a total of no more than $40$ pounds. Each box loaded onto it weighs $3$ pounds. What is the greatest number of boxes that can be loaded onto the cart?
hint: Part of the limit is already used up by the equipment. Think about which symbol matches the phrase no more than.

hints.text: Part of the limit is already used up by the equipment. Think about which symbol matches the phrase no more than.
With $b$ boxes the total weight is $3b + 7$, and it must satisfy $3b + 7 \le 40$. Subtract $7$, then divide by $3$.
This gives $3b \le 33$, so $b \le 11$. The greatest number of boxes is $11$.

learningObjective: Translate a capacity constraint into an inequality and interpret the result.
explanation: The phrase no more than $40$ means the total can equal $40$ or be less. With $b$ boxes the total weight is $3b + 7$.
Write and solve the inequality: $3b + 7 \le 40$ gives $3b \le 33$, so $b \le 11$.
Boxes are whole objects, and $11$ boxes weigh $3(11) + 7 = 40$ pounds, exactly at the limit. The greatest number of boxes is $11$.

alternativeExplanations.title: Reason with the remaining capacity
steps: Of the $40$-pound limit, $7$ pounds is already used, leaving $33$ pounds.
When the division comes out even, the boundary value is achievable — "no more than" allows equality, so $11$ works rather than $10$.
